passages.where: A man sick in body and weighed down by guilt says he is bent low, mourning all day, numb and badly crushed. The site's plain note says he believed his illness was tied to his sin, and that the psalm does not teach that every illness is a punishment. The word numb stands in Scripture inside a prayer, spoken to God rather than about him.

When his sons tell Jacob that Joseph is alive and rules Egypt, the shock is too great: the site's note says his heart goes numb and he does not believe them. Only when he hears all that Joseph said and sees the wagons does his spirit revive. Numbness can come from too much at once, even from news a person had stopped hoping for, and it can lift by degrees.

David and his men come home to find Ziklag burned and their families carried off, and they weep until they have no strength left to weep. The site's note on the chapter says that while his own men talk of stoning him, David strengthens himself in the LORD. Scripture records a grief that empties a person of tears, and none of them is rebuked for it.

Far from the temple and mocked by those who ask where his God is, a worshiper asks his own soul why it is downcast and tells it to hope in God. The site's plain note says a believer is allowed to feel downcast, and that he does not only listen to his feelings but talks back to them. It is not pretending to be fine; it is choosing where to look while still low.

David's spirit grows faint and his heart is dismayed, and he remembers the days of old and stretches out his hands to God like parched land. The site's plain note calls the psalm a model of prayer from the bottom of a hard time, which remembers what God has done and reaches out to him. Empty hands held out to God are still held out.

Its heading calls this the prayer of one who is afflicted and grows faint, and the sufferer says his days vanish like smoke and his heart is withered like grass, so that he forgets to eat. The site's plain note says the psalm was written for a person on their worst day. Forgetting to eat and losing sleep are signs the note says should not be carried alone.

The man of Lamentations says his soul has been deprived of peace and he has forgotten what prosperity is, and then he deliberately calls something to mind: the LORD's mercies are new every morning. The site's note says the chapter does not solve the tension between his affliction and God's goodness but lives inside it. Hope here is remembered on purpose before it is felt.

Paul says the Spirit helps believers in their weakness, because they do not know how they ought to pray, and the Spirit himself intercedes for them with groans too deep for words. The site's plain note asks what it would mean to bring God even a wordless sigh. A person who cannot find a feeling to pray from is not praying alone.

God presents his Servant, who brings justice quietly and gently and will not break a bruised reed or put out a smoldering wick. The site's note says the New Testament applies this song directly to Jesus, and Matthew quotes it of his healing. A wick that only smolders is not thrown away.

Seeing Mary and the mourners weeping, Jesus is deeply moved and troubled, and he weeps. The site's note calls these verses the fullest picture of Jesus' emotions in the Gospels, and the plain note says grief is not unbelief. The one who comes near the numb is not numb himself.

misread.taken: Rejoice at all times is quoted to people who feel flat or empty as if a Christian should always feel glad, so that feeling nothing is itself a failure of faith.
misread.says: The site's plain note says rejoicing at all times is not pretending: Paul wept, worried and grieved, and said so in his letters, and joy in Christ can sit beside sorrow without cancelling it. It says that if sadness has settled on a person and will not lift, these verses do not shame them, and that when it lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise and is not a failure of faith.

whole: If the numbness has come with thoughts of hurting yourself, or has taken your sleep, your appetite or your days for weeks, tell someone you trust today, a doctor, a pastor or a friend, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Feeling nothing can be part of depression, which is an illness and not a failure of faith. Numbness is hard to describe because it is the absence of something. People say the days pass without touching them, that music and worship and the faces of the people they love reach them as if through glass, that they could not cry when they expected to and cannot laugh when others do. Some are frightened by it; some are too tired to be frightened. Christians often carry a second weight on top of it: the fear that a heart which feels nothing toward God must be a hard heart, or that their faith has gone.

Scripture knows this state from the inside. A sick man in Psalm 38 says he is numb and badly crushed. Jacob, told after many years that Joseph was alive, was stunned and could not believe it. David and his men wept at Ziklag until they had no strength left to weep, and the sufferer of Psalm 102 forgot to eat. None of them is rebuked for it in the text. Sometimes numbness is what a person feels when there has been too much: too much loss, too much fear, too many years of carrying something alone. Sometimes it is illness in the body and the mind. Often it is both, and it is easy for the person inside it to read it as a verdict on their soul when it is closer to the exhaustion of a heart that has been overwhelmed.

So the Bible's wisdom does not begin by demanding a feeling. The singer of Psalm 42 talks to his own downcast soul and tells it to hope in God; the man of Lamentations calls to mind the mercies that are new every morning before he says he feels them; David in Psalm 143 remembers the days of old and stretches out his hands like dry ground. Paul says that when we do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays for us with groans too deep for words, so a wordless sigh still counts. Small things are faithful here: eating, sleeping, staying near people who do not need you to perform, reading a psalm aloud when you cannot pray in your own words. And numbness that lasts deserves a doctor's attention as much as a pain that lasts, and asking for that help is not a lack of faith.

The hope Scripture gives is a Servant who does not put out a smoldering wick. Jesus stood with the mourners at Bethany and wept, and the one who comes near the numb is not numb himself. Jacob's spirit revived when he saw the wagons; feeling can come back by degrees, and sometimes it comes back as grief before it comes back as joy. Until it does, you are not measured by what you can feel. The LORD's mercies are new every morning whether or not you sense them, and they will be there again tomorrow.
sit: What would it be like to tell God plainly that you feel nothing, and to let that honest sentence be your prayer today?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note on Psalm 42 says the poem does not end with the problem solved, and to read on into Psalm 43, which finishes it. Pray its last lines when you cannot find words of your own; the refrain still says downcast, and it still says hope.

careLines.text: If you are like the man in this psalm, unable to sleep, forgetting to eat, feeling alone like a bird on a roof, please do not carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
When grief or sadness lasts and starts taking sleep, appetite or work, seeing a doctor is wise, and it is not a failure of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
